turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Good morning, this is The Morning Commute. Friday, August 14th. I'm Sam.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And I'm Alex. Wall Street's two straight record closes give way to a quiet Friday tape, and China's own July data just confirmed both its export and consumption legs are cooling at once.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: But the real thread today is physical, not financial — the AI buildout keeps running into land, copper and steel. A 550-foot easement dispute is stranding a full gigawatt of finished Colorado wind, and Texas's own demand forecaster says most of the large loads chasing power there won't actually have it by 2030.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the same day Bloomberg flags Texas's own governor cooling on the data-center deals he was championing less than a year ago. And in the Philippines, a fresh graft number just landed — 24 billion pesos, straight out of the public-works budget.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Plenty to get through. Let's start with the world.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Iran's joint military command declared yesterday that no vessel can transit the Strait of Hormuz without Tehran's permission — flatly rejecting Trump's claim of "total control" over the strait.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Senior political-military official Rasoul Sanaei-Rad went further, saying Iran won't actually reopen the strait until the US meets its commitments under last month's interim deal. Shipping traffic through Hormuz is reportedly sitting at three-month lows.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's a genuinely different posture from where we left this story — Tehran isn't just stalling on reparations anymore, it's publicly contesting the basic premise that the US has any control there at all.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Which matters beyond the optics — it's the same oil-price uncertainty that's now showing up directly in the Philippines peso, which we'll get to.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Second story — US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, a longtime settlement-movement ally, called an Israeli settler siege in the West Bank town of Qusra an "act of terror" yesterday.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Settlers besieged three Palestinian homes — including one belonging to a US citizen — trapping around fifteen people, two of them children, without power or water for days. Israel's military dismantled two outposts and detained one Israeli in response.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The word choice is the story here. American officials essentially never apply "terrorist" to settlers — that language is reserved for the other side. Coming from Huckabee specifically, of all people, it's a real signal.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Worth watching whether that language holds or gets walked back in the next news cycle. Either way, it's a notable crack in a normally very disciplined US line.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And it lands at an awkward moment for Washington generally — an administration trying to hold together both a fragile Gaza framework and a stalled Hormuz track can't really afford its own ambassador freelancing on language this loaded, even in service of a legitimate rebuke.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two stories, same underlying pattern really — actors testing exactly how far rhetoric can move before it forces an actual policy response.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: On the tape — Thursday was record number two in a row. S&P 500 closed at 7,798.99, up 0.65%, its first close above 7,800. Nasdaq 26,803.03, up 0.81%, led by Meta, Micron and Netflix.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Dow barely moved, up 0.13% to 53,839.99. Russell 2000 up 0.24% to 3,052.85. Ten-year sitting at 4.68% — that print's actually two days stale, nothing fresher available this morning, so take it as a marker, not gospel.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Oil's flat — Brent 87.18, up just 0.13%. WTI around 81.30, essentially unchanged. Gold down slightly, 4,407.50, off 0.29% — no safe-haven bid despite the Hormuz rhetoric.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Today's tape looks genuinely quiet after that — Europe's mixed, FTSE down 0.3%, CAC flat, DAX actually up half a percent bucking the trend. Asia's mixed too, and US futures are little-changed heading in.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: No fresh catalyst overnight — Thursday's CPI-driven record run is still the story propping up sentiment. Today's just digestion.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Worth flagging the stale ten-year print again, because it matters for how you read today — if yields actually moved meaningfully since Wednesday, this calm surface could be hiding more than it's showing. We'll know for certain by Monday.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Until then, treat today as a hold-your-breath session — nothing's forcing a move either way, and that's exactly the kind of tape where a single surprise headline does outsized damage.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two AI-infrastructure earnings landed Thursday and went in completely opposite directions. Super Micro rallied more than 6% on a blowout guide — adjusted EPS of 1.01 to 1.10 dollars against a 76-cent consensus, revenue guide of 14.5 to 15.5 billion.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Cerebras went the other way, down 14% after Q2 revenue of 180 million missed the 194 million estimate. Same AI-datacenter trade, same week, completely different verdict — the pattern we've tracked all summer on hyperscaler earnings, just one tier down the supply chain now.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Second story — Thoma Bravo is taking insurance platform Accelerant Holdings private, 20.25 dollars a share cash, a 49% premium to Wednesday's close. Deal's worth more than 4 billion.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Largest holder Altamont Capital, which controls about 82% of the vote, has already agreed to support it, so this isn't speculative — expected to close in the first half of 2027.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Another name on a take-private list that's gotten genuinely long this year. Once a board and a controlling shareholder are aligned like this, the stock just trades to the deal price and stops reacting to anything else.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Two very different sectors, same underlying signal — capital's getting more selective and more decisive at the same time. Reward conviction fast, punish a miss fast, and take a whole company off the public market the moment control and price line up.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: In Japan — the Bank of Japan's July meeting summary flagged rising inflation risk, with at least one board member floating a faster hike pace than markets had priced.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Yen firmed on it, about 0.2% to 159.15 against the dollar — pulling back from the 160 level that's become the market's informal intervention trigger. July producer prices came in at 7.2% year-on-year, just under the 7.4% forecast and down slightly from June.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: So the signal's consistent — inflation's still hot enough in Japan that a "faster than expected" framing from the BOJ carries real weight, even without an actual move yet.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Meanwhile the UK posted its seventh straight quarter of GDP growth — up 0.4% in the second quarter, services doing the work at plus 0.5%, construction up 0.3%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: But retail and wholesale trade were flat for the quarter — zero growth — even with the Bank of England holding at 3.75% since July 30th and June CPI down to 2.6%. Consumer confidence is still deeply negative, negative 17, even though that's up six points.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Same story in two different economies, really — headline growth or headline inflation moving the way policymakers want, while the consumer-facing part of the economy lags behind and doesn't feel it yet.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Worth remembering that gap the next time a GDP print gets read as unambiguously good news — the retail number sitting right next to it is telling a much flatter story.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And in China — today's July activity data from the National Bureau of Statistics missed on both legs at once. Industrial production up 5.7% year-on-year, below the 6% forecast and down sharply from June's 6.8%.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Retail sales missed too. The read-through on industrial production specifically is that front-loaded export demand — factories rushing shipments out ahead of US tariff deadlines — is fading now that the rush is over.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which means you can't blame this one purely on external demand. Retail missing in the same release means the domestic consumer leg is cooling right alongside the export leg, at the same time, not offsetting it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's the more worrying combination for Beijing than either number alone — a slowdown showing up on both the making-things side and the buying-things side simultaneously usually takes more than one policy lever to fix.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: We'll come back to China's growth question through a very different lens later. For now, let's go deep on today's Deep Dive.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Today's Deep Dive comes from a feature in The Generalist newsletter — Part Two of a series called "Saplings," this installment titled "Unstable Ground." It's not a markets story at all, and it's a genuinely good one.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The series studies the early lives of legendary founders, looking for patterns in what shaped them before they built anything. Part Two is specifically about the home — the kind of instability that recurs again and again in these childhoods.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The opening story is Amadeo Giannini, who founded what became Bank of America. In 1876, when he was six years old, he watched a farmhand shoot his father dead in a dispute over a dollar of unpaid wages. That night, his mother told him: "This is the last time I take you on my knees. From today, you are the man of the house."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That pattern — early loss, followed by an abrupt inheritance of adult responsibility — shows up across an enormous list of names. Stan Shih of Acer, George Eastman of Kodak, Fred Smith of FedEx, Jerry Yang of Yahoo, Carlos Slim, Aristotle Onassis, Harland Sanders of KFC, James Dyson, Jim Casey of UPS — all lost a parent in childhood or adolescence.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Li Ka-Shing's version is almost identical to Giannini's. His father was dying of tuberculosis when Li was fifteen, and told him "a man must have ambitions." Li promised him, in tears, "I will learn to do business and make lots of money" — and within three years had gone from sweeping factory floors to the company's star salesman.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Jorge Paulo Lemann's father was struck and killed by a streetcar when Lemann was fourteen — the same immediate shift into being "the man of the house." The piece's argument is that parental death doesn't just create grief, it compresses childhood into a kind of forced adulthood, and pushes the bereaved child to rely entirely on themselves earlier than anyone should have to.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Not every case in the piece is death, either. Larry Ellison found out he was adopted at around twelve, over dinner, with zero elaboration — his words later were something like, "It was like, 'Tonight we're having meatloaf, and by the way, you're adopted.'" No trauma of loss, but the same effect — the story he'd been standing on turned out not to be true.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And then there's Ted Turner, whose father agreed to sell part of the family business and then killed himself the very next day, when Turner was twenty-four. Turner spent the rest of his life visibly obsessed with mortality — friends describe him talking about his own potential suicide constantly, almost flippantly, for years afterward.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The author's framing, and it's a fair one, is that this isn't a checklist for producing a founder — it's not statistical, it doesn't claim causation. It's an accounting of a pattern he finds genuinely meaningful: early loss, a disappointing father paired with a more dominant mother, love that had to be earned rather than given freely, status that moved rather than stayed fixed, and family expectations placed on a child's shoulders before they were old enough to choose them.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: What I find most useful about it isn't the individual anecdotes, dramatic as they are — it's the throughline that instability absorbed very young seems to produce a particular relationship to risk later. If you've already learned as a child that your circumstances can change completely overnight, taking a big swing as an adult doesn't feel as reckless as it would to someone who never had that lesson forced on them.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: There's a less romantic reading too, worth holding alongside the inspiring one — survivorship bias is doing real work in a piece like this. Nobody's writing a "Saplings" essay about the thousand kids who lost a parent young and didn't found anything. We only hear about the instability when it's attached to an eventual bank or an airline.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Fair, and the author actually flags that himself — this isn't a formula, it's a study of the people who happened to become extraordinary, read backward. Still worth the read for what it says about risk tolerance and self-reliance, even if you're skeptical of drawing a straight line from childhood loss to entrepreneurial success.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: It's a good palate-cleanser before we head back into markets — a reminder that behind every one of these company names is an actual person shaped by something that happened decades before the first product ever launched.

segments.raw: SEGMENT TWO — ENERGY / DATA CENTERS / UTILITIES
segments.label: Energy / Data Centers / Utilities

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Staying with something structural — this time the AI buildout itself. In Colorado, Xcel's regulated utility PSCo is asking the state Supreme Court to unlock eminent domain powers over a single gen-tie line, and the numbers behind it are wild.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Two wind farms — Singing Grass at 603 megawatts and Cheyenne Ridge Two at 450 — are sitting essentially finished, about 1.05 gigawatts and something like 1.8 billion dollars of capital, stranded over a dispute involving roughly 550 feet of easement.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: A district court ruled back in June that Colorado law doesn't let a regulated utility condemn land for a generation-tie line the way it can for public transmission — the reasoning being a gen-tie serves one private project, not the grid broadly. So PSCo can't force the last landowner to sell.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And PSCo didn't help its own case — it reportedly offered under 20,000 dollars for that 550-foot segment, when it paid 585,000 dollars for 90 acres in the same general area back in 2022, and NextEra settled with that very same landowner at market rate for its nearby Dusty Rose project.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the real story underneath the legal one — a utility trying to lowball the one landowner it actually needs, and now two nearly-finished wind farms are stuck because of it. Colorado's legislature already moved back in March to curb Xcel's eminent domain power generally, so the political wind is against them too.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The practitioner read here is that this becomes real precedent — if the Supreme Court agrees a gen-tie doesn't count as public use, every last-mile landowner in Colorado, and in states with similar statutes, just gained enormous leverage over interconnection routing. That's a chokepoint that has nothing to do with queue reform or turbine supply.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Speaking of turbine supply — Mitsubishi Power's gas turbine backlog just hit 35 gigawatts, up 52% year-on-year, and orders booked this quarter are already slotting into 2028 through 2030 delivery.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Put that next to what we already know — Siemens Energy sitting around 70 gigawatts, GE Vernova at 116. All three major OEMs are now effectively fully booked into the next decade. This isn't one company being cautious, it's the entire global turbine supply chain maxed out at once.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: There's a second bottleneck getting far less attention than turbines, though, and it might matter more. A startup called Heron Power, founded by an ex-Tesla battery executive, is building a 100-million-dollar factory outside San Jose to mass-produce a chip-based, software-controlled alternative to the standard steel-and-oil grid transformer.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Standard transformers are running lead times of up to four years right now — arguably the single biggest hardware chokepoint behind interconnection delays, longer even than the turbine wait. Heron's targeting mass production of its solid-state unit by late 2027, more than 600 jobs, up to 10,000 units a year at full run rate.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Whether silicon actually beats copper and steel at this scale remains to be proven — but it's a genuinely different kind of bet than anything else we've covered in this space, substituting semiconductors for heavy industrial manufacturing rather than just trying to build more of the same thing faster.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And Texas just handed us the clearest evidence yet that all of this matters. ERCOT hit a new all-time peak demand of 91.1 gigawatts on July 22nd, 6% above the old record — but Ascend Analytics is now warning that more than 80% of the new large loads chasing power in Texas won't actually have matching generation online by 2030.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The interconnection queue has grown by over 200 gigawatts since 2024, and Ascend puts the realistic completion rate at only about 55%. So even setting aside the politics of the queue-cull fight we've covered before, there's a hard physical cap here — roughly half the projects that get through the process still won't have power to run on.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Three different bottlenecks, three different fixes being tried — a legal fight over 550 feet of land, a chip company betting against a four-year transformer wait, and a state grid operator's own forecaster admitting the math doesn't work at current build rates. None of them are about capital anymore. Capital's the one input in this cycle that's never actually been the constraint.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: In the Philippines — a genuinely fresh corruption story broke this week, and it's a big number. Former DPWH Secretary Manuel Bonoan testified before the Sandiganbayan on Tuesday that every single senator received a share of what he called a 24-billion-peso "leadership fund" tucked into the 2025 Department of Public Works budget.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: At least 500 million pesos per senator, up to a billion for committee chairs, according to the testimony. Senate President Migz Zubiri is disputing that 24-billion figure outright, and Senator Panfilo Lacson renewed his call to abolish the fund entirely yesterday, calling it — his words — "not pork barrel, worse."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The Palace weighed in today too — spokesperson Claire Castro said Marcos has "no personal knowledge" of the fund, and that nothing like it exists in the 2027 budget currently before Congress.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: "No personal knowledge" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. It answers a much narrower question than the one everyone's actually asking, and it leaves the door open either way depending on what investigators turn up next.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: On the economic side, the peso closed at 61.343 to the dollar Thursday, down about 16 centavos, its weakest level in two weeks. The driver ties directly back to our first headline today — the stalled US-Iran talks are pushing oil and the dollar higher together, and the Philippines imports essentially all of its oil.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: BSP Governor Eli Remolona put a fresh, notably more sanguine spin on that same growth number today, calling it "disappointing, but not that bad" — a softer read than the central bank's tone when the 2.3% print first landed. He says weak growth gives room to ease up on tightening, but wants clearer disinflation evidence before actually doing that.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Here's the tension worth flagging, though — Citi's own economists are still penciling in two more 25-basis-point hikes this year, in August and October, landing the policy rate at 5.25% by year-end. So Remolona's public tone right now is running noticeably softer than what the market's own forecasters still expect the BSP to actually do.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Quick status check on the impeachment trial, since we've been following it closely — day fifteen wrapped Tuesday with the Senate adjourning after a sharp clash between the defense and prosecution over COA testimony. Next session isn't until Monday the 17th, so nothing new to report there today.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Skipping the PSEi today too — it fell about 1.2% on profit-taking and the weaker peso, a routine move, not the kind of swing worth spending time on. And no active weather signal from PAGASA right now, so we'll leave that alone as well.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: The throughline across both Philippine stories today is really about how much external pressure keeps landing on a country managing its own accountability problems at the same time — Hormuz uncertainty hitting the currency from outside, a fresh graft number complicating the politics from inside.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: And the two aren't actually separate problems, either — a weaker peso raises the landed cost of everything the government imports for its own infrastructure programs, which is the exact same budget the leadership-fund allegations are about. External pressure doesn't just sit next to the domestic story, it makes the domestic story more expensive to fix.

segments.raw: SEGMENT FOUR — VOCAB OF THE DAY
segments.label: Vocab Of The Day

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 好，来看看今天的两个中文词。第一个跟今天的能源新闻有关——"不容忽视"。

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: "不容忽视"的意思是"cannot be tolerated to be ignored"，也就是不能被忽视。今天Ascend Analytics的报告说，到2030年，得州超过八成的大型用电项目可能拿不到匹配的发电量——这个风险不容忽视。

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 翻译过来就是：this risk cannot be ignored — by 2030, more than 80% of Texas's large power projects may not have matching generation available。

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: "不容忽视"是比较正式的书面语，常用在政策报告、分析师笔记里，后面常搭配"问题"、"风险"、"趋势"。跟"值得关注"比，"不容忽视"语气强得多——"值得关注"只是提醒你注意，"不容忽视"是警告你，不管它后果会很严重。

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 第二个词跟中国今天的经济数据有关——"由此可见"。

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: "由此可见"的意思是"from this it can be seen that"，专门用来从已经摆出的事实里推出结论。今天中国七月的工业增加值和零售数据同时不及预期，可以说：由此可见，出口和消费两方面同时放缓，问题不只是外部需求。

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 翻译：from this it can be seen that both exports and consumption are slowing at the same time — this isn't just an external-demand problem。

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: "由此可见"是很正式的过渡词，一般放在句子开头，专门总结前面的证据。比简单的"可见"更强调推理过程；平时聊天更常直接说"看来"或者"看样子"，没有这么严谨的论证语气。

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: 好，从中文换到菲律宾语。Ngayon, tara na sa Tagalog. Una, "katiwalian."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: "Katiwalian" ay nangangahulugang corruption o malfeasance — hindi lang basta pangungurakot, kundi ang pang-aabuso ng tiwalang ibinigay sa isang opisyal. Halimbawa: Idinetalye ni dating DPWH Sekretaryo Bonoan ang umano'y katiwalian sa 24-bilyong-pisong "leadership fund."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ibig sabihin: former DPWH Secretary Bonoan detailed the alleged corruption in the 24-billion-peso "leadership fund." Iyan mismo ang balitang sumabog ngayong linggo.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: "Katiwalian" ay mas malakas at mas pormal kaysa sa kolokyal na "korap" — ang "korap" parang tsismis o kaswal na akusasyon, habang ang "katiwalian" ang salitang ginagamit sa balita, sa investigative reports, at sa mismong kaso sa Sandiganbayan.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Pangalawa, "pag-aalinlangan."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: "Pag-aalinlangan" ay nangangahulugang hesitation o uncertainty — ang pagdududa kung dapat kumilos o hindi. Halimbawa: Dahil sa mahinang GDP, nasa pag-aalinlangan ang BSP kung ipagpapatuloy pa nila ang mahigpit na patakaran sa interes.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Ibig sabihin: because of the weak GDP print, the BSP is in a state of hesitation over whether to continue its tight interest-rate policy.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Ang pagkakaiba ng "pag-aalinlangan" sa mas kaswal na "medyo nag-aalangan" — ang una ay isang mas matimbang, mas institusyonal na pag-aatubili, habang ang huli ay parang personal at pang-araw-araw na pagdududa lang.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Magandang pares din ito — isang salita tungkol sa katiwalian sa pulitika, isa tungkol sa pag-aalinlangan sa patakarang pang-ekonomiya. Pareho namang tungkol sa mga desisyong ginagawa — o hindi ginagawa — sa likod ng saradong pinto.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Arts and culture — starting with the auction world's biggest single-collection news this year. Sotheby's has landed the Blaquier collection, the Impressionist and post-Impressionist holdings of the late Argentine industrialists Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and Carlos Pedro Blaquier, beating out Christie's with a guarantee.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's heading to a dedicated November sale in New York, and the headline lot is a Van Gogh — "Châtaignier en fleurs roses et blanches" from 1890, estimated at 150 to 200 million dollars. There's also a Cézanne from his Harlequin series estimated above 120 million, plus Degas, Pissarro and Renoir works each expected above 25 million.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: This is exactly the kind of generational-wealth-transfer consignment the market's been waiting for to power an autumn recovery — one collection, assembled over decades by a single family, hitting the block all at once.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: In museums — the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art finally opens September 22nd in Los Angeles's Exposition Park, after roughly a decade of construction and years before that spent finding a city willing to host it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: George Lucas has framed it explicitly as "a museum for the people" — but the twenty-five-dollar adult admission is drawing real pushback given that framing, especially sitting next to LA's mostly-free major institutions. The museum's partial answer is offering free access to residents of the neighboring 90037 zip code specifically.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: It's a genuinely unusual collection, too — narrative and figurative art spanning illustration, animation, comic art and film alongside more traditional painting, built almost entirely from Lucas's own decades of private collecting. Worth watching whether that zip-code carve-out becomes a template other billionaire-funded museums start copying, or stays a one-off gesture tied to this specific neighborhood.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: And in opera — Decca just released the world-premiere recording of an opera that's been lost for almost a hundred and forty years. Umberto Giordano wrote "Marina" at twenty-one, for the same 1888 competition that Mascagni ended up winning with "Cavalleria Rusticana."

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Giordano shelved it after losing, folded some of the music into a later opera, and it just sat there. The actual world-premiere staging happened this past February at Teatro Dal Verme in Milan, and the recording pairs Eleonora Buratto in the title role with tenor Freddie De Tommaso.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Gramophone called it "a triumph" in this month's issue. There's something genuinely rare about a work getting its actual premiere a hundred and thirty-eight years after it was written, rather than just being revived from an existing performance history — this is Giordano's music meeting an audience for the very first time.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Op-eds today — Ben Casselman, the New York Times's chief economics correspondent, published a piece called "AI Is Reshaping the Economy, but the Data Can't Keep Up."

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: His steelman is basically intellectual honesty about uncertainty — official government statistics were built for a slower, pre-AI economy, response rates to surveys keep falling, and the agencies collecting this data are themselves underfunded. He points to the Yale Budget Lab's occupational-churn tracker, which so far finds no clear link between AI adoption and job losses — and notably, the firms investing the most in AI are actually hiring faster, not shedding workers.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The counter is that waiting for clean, aggregate data to settle the question is itself a choice, and it favors inaction. AI-attributed layoffs at Amazon, Salesforce, Meta, Accenture and IBM topped roughly 50,000 in a single bad month last October, and companies are increasingly naming AI explicitly in their layoff filings even if economists can't yet prove causation in the topline numbers.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: "Too soon to tell" can be a genuinely honest position, but it can also quietly become a permanent alibi — the data will always lag the disruption it's trying to measure, and by the time it's clean enough to be certain, the disruption's already happened to the people it happened to.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Second piece — Liam Denning at Bloomberg Opinion, "When Texas Cools on AI Data Centers, Big Tech Has a Problem," published yesterday.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: His steelman ties directly into our energy segment today. Governor Abbott stood on a stage with Alphabet's Sundar Pichai less than a year ago, calling Texas the epicenter of AI development — and now he's visibly cooler on the buildout, as grid strain, local opposition and ratepayer anger have all sharpened. Denning's point is that if even the most AI-friendly state in the country is hedging, that's a leading indicator for how hyperscalers should be pricing political risk everywhere else.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: The counter is that local friction in one or two counties isn't the same thing as statewide policy risk. ERCOT's market structure and a genuinely pro-growth legislature both have strong incentives to keep courting hyperscaler tax revenue, and the actual grid buildout — the turbines, the transformers, the interconnection fights we just covered — keeps proceeding regardless of one governor's rhetorical mood.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Read those two together with everything else in today's show, and there's a real pattern — the AI story keeps getting harder to cleanly measure or cleanly predict, on the labor-market side and the political-support side both, exactly while the physical buildout underneath it keeps moving forward on its own momentum regardless.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Which might be the most honest one-line summary of where this cycle actually is right now — nobody can prove the disruption yet, nobody can stop the buildout yet, and both of those things are true for the same underlying reason: reality's simply moving faster than anyone's ability to measure or govern it.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: One good thing today — a postcard that took twenty-six years to arrive.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Bob Sheppard, in Long Beach, California, opened his mailbox this week and found a postcard his parents had mailed him from Copenhagen back in July of 2000. Signed simply "M and D" — Mom and Dad.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Both of his parents have since passed — his mother four years ago, his father six years ago. The postal service has no real explanation for where it sat for a quarter of a century, or why it finally moved now.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: There's something genuinely lovely about a small, ordinary piece of mail outlasting the two people who sent it, and then landing in exactly the right hands anyway, decades later than planned.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: Sheppard said it felt like hearing from them again, out of nowhere, on an otherwise completely normal day. Sometimes the good thing really is just that simple.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: That's the show for today.

turns.speaker: SAM
turns.text: That's The Morning Commute. We'll see you tomorrow.

turns.speaker: ALEX
turns.text: Take care, everyone.
